summary: The SIP event notification framework lets users subscribe to changes in a resource but lacks a way to filter them. This document describes what subscribers do to attach filtering rules to a subscription, how responses and filtered notifications are handled, and how notifiers behave. It was later updated by RFC 6665.

The subscriber writes a filter saying which parts of the resource state to receive and which changes to be told about. The server then sends less data, which matters on slow, small devices.

subtitle: How SIP subscribers attach filters to a subscription and how notifiers and list servers must honour them.

tldr.problem: The SIP event notification framework lets a subscriber follow changes to a resource but gives it no way to limit what a notification contains or when it is sent, which is costly on slow, small devices.
tldr.mechanism: The subscriber puts an XML filter in the body of the SUBSCRIBE request; the what part selects the content of each notification and the trigger part decides which changes trigger one, and a resource list server routes each filter to the back-end subscriptions it belongs to.
tldr.outcome: It defines the subscriber, list server and notifier behaviour, the error handling and the security limits, including a recommended limit of 40 filter elements per request. It was later updated by RFC 6665.

facts.label: Recommended element limit
facts.value: 40 occurrences of what, changed, added and removed

today: RFC 4660 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2006. It has not been obsoleted, but it was updated by RFC 6665.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The SIP event notification framework, described in RFC 3265, defines a general framework for sending subscriptions and receiving notifications in SIP-based systems. It introduces the concept of event packages, which are concrete applications of the general event framework to a specific usage of events.

That framework does not describe a mechanism whereby filtering of event notification information can be achieved. Filtering is a mechanism for controlling the content of event notifications, and it also lets the subscriber specify the rules for when a notification should be sent to it. The RFC expects the mechanism to be particularly valuable to users of mobile wireless access devices, whose characteristics typically include high latency, low bandwidth, low data processing capabilities, small displays and limited battery power. Such devices can benefit from the ability to filter the amount of information generated at the source of the event notification, but implementers need to be aware of the computational burden this places on that source.

The framework states that the notifier may send a NOTIFY at any time, but that it is typically sent when the state of the resource changes, and that notifications contain the complete and current state of the resource authorized for a certain subscriber to see. The format of that resource state information is package specific. This document assumes that the NOTIFY for any package contains an XML document.

This document, together with RFC 4661, presents a mechanism for filtering whereby a subscriber describes its preference for when notifications are to be sent to it and what they are to contain. It also describes how the notifier functions when generating notifications, taking into account filters and the default functionality of the package or service. The XML format for defining the filter is described in RFC 4661.
sections.plainLanguage: The SIP event notification framework lets a program subscribe to changes in a resource, but it has no way to say how much of each notification to send. This document adds that. The subscriber writes a filter saying which parts of the resource state to receive and which changes to be told about. The server then sends less data, which matters on slow, small devices.

sections.title: The Subscriber's SUBSCRIBE Request
sections.content:
The filter travels to the server by inserting the XML document, as defined in RFC 4661, in the body of the SUBSCRIBE request. Alternatively the document can be uploaded to the server by means outside the scope of this document. SIP entities compliant with this specification MUST support the content type application/simple-filter+xml.

The SUBSCRIBE message MAY contain a body, and that body would carry filtering information. Honouring those filters is at the discretion of the notifier and might depend on local policies. No content in the body of a SUBSCRIBE indicates to the notifier that no filter is being requested, so the notifier is instructed to send all the NOTIFY requests using the notifier's own or service-specific policy. If the body of the SUBSCRIBE does include the filter, the body MUST be of the MIME type application/simple-filter+xml.

Multiple filters MAY be included in one SUBSCRIBE, by including multiple <filter> elements in the filter. Each <filter> element may include a uri attribute. A SUBSCRIBE request destined to a list URI MAY include multiple filters specific to individual resources, achieved by including multiple <filter> elements with different resource URIs in each of those elements. These resource-specific filters are processed first, before any list-specific filter, if any. Regardless of whether the SUBSCRIBE is destined to a list URI, there can only be one filter applicable to a single resource or domain within a single SUBSCRIBE: each filter within a subscription MUST uniquely identify one resource or one domain. A filter can be enabled and disabled using the enabled attribute in the <filter> element.

The subscriber of the filter MUST ensure that the XML document inserted as the SUBSCRIBE request body is well formed and valid, and MUST NOT insert any extension elements or attributes unless it has access to the extension schema and can validate the document. The notifier MAY validate the XML document according to the schemas, including extension schemas, to which it has access that are applicable to it.
sections.plainLanguage: The subscriber puts the filter in the body of the SUBSCRIBE request, using the content type application/simple-filter+xml. A SUBSCRIBE with no body asks for everything, which is the notifier's own choice. A SUBSCRIBE may carry several filters at once, but each filter must point at a different resource or domain. The subscriber must check that its XML is well formed before sending it.

sections.title: Request-URI versus Filter URI
sections.content:
The URI in the filter defines the target resource. In the Presence service case it is the presentity's presence information to which the filter is applied. The subscriber MAY choose to leave the URI in the filter undefined, in which case the filter applies to the resource identified in the Request-URI. The subscriber MAY also define a filter URI. If the Request-URI is a list URI, the filter URI MUST be the list URI, a sub-list URI, or a resource whose URI is one of the URIs that result from a lookup, by a Resource List Server, on the Request-URI. If it is not, the filter may be ignored or may be rejected. URI matching is done according to the matching rules defined for a particular scheme, and the SIP URI matching rules are defined in RFC 3261.

A filter may also be addressed to a domain using the domain attribute instead of the uri attribute, in which case the filter applies to resources in that domain. This can be used when a subscription is for a resource that is an event list with many resources from differing domains. If an individual resource-specific filter is present along with the domain filter, that resource-specific filter overrides the domain-specific filter.
sections.plainLanguage: Each filter says what it applies to. It can name one resource by its URI, or name a whole domain. If it names neither, it applies to the resource named in the SUBSCRIBE request itself. A filter for one resource always wins over a filter for a domain.

sections.title: Changing Filters within a Dialog
sections.content:
The subscriber MAY reset or change the filter by re-issuing a new SUBSCRIBE request within the existing dialog. A SUBSCRIBE within the existing dialog that does not contain a filter is assumed to maintain existing filters, so filters are persistent within a dialog and are only explicitly removed. A subscriber requiring removal of a filter may do so by using the remove="true" attribute.

Where the URI in the filter is that of a list, a subscriber may override the existing filter with a filter for an individual resource that is part of the list subscribed to earlier, by issuing a new SUBSCRIBE within the existing dialog and including a filter specific for that individual resource, using a new filter ID. The new filter need not include the original filter, since a filter is only removed in the manner described above.

A filter is replaced by the subscriber re-issuing the filter using the same filter ID and replacing the contents of the filter. Replacing a filter by changing the filter ID and keeping the resource URI is considered an error, since this causes the server to assume that two filters are placed for the same resource. A filter can also be disabled and re-enabled using the enabled attribute in the <filter> element.
sections.plainLanguage: Filters last for the life of the subscription. A new SUBSCRIBE inside the same dialog changes them: the same filter ID replaces the old filter, a new ID adds another one, and remove="true" takes a filter away. Keeping the same resource URI but changing the filter ID is an error.

sections.title: Resource List Server Behaviour
sections.content:
The Resource List Server, defined in RFC 4663, fans a subscription to a list out into subscriptions to the individual resources in that list. This section describes how such an entity behaves when a filter is present in a subscription to a list.

If the URI is not defined within the filter, or the filter's URI matches the Request-URI of the SUBSCRIBE request, the filter applies to all the notifications that the RLS issues to the subscription. If the URI indicated by the filter is for one resource whose URI is one of the URIs that result from a lookup by the RLS on the Request-URI, the filter for that particular resource is extracted and propagated in the SUBSCRIBE request sent to that resource; where a SUBSCRIBE carries more than one filter, a filter specific to a resource MUST be extracted and only that one propagated. If the URI indicated by the filter is for one resource whose URI is NOT under the RLS administrative control, the RLS propagates the filter to all the fanned-out subscriptions, to cover the case where the subscriber knows that there are sub-lists in the event list that are under a different administrative domain. If the URI indicated by the filter is for one resource whose URI is under the RLS administrative control but is not part of the resource list that the subscription was addressed to, the filter is not propagated, and it is the RLS's responsibility to make sure that this filter is applied to notifications it issues, if information about that resource is present.

A filter addressed to a domain with the domain attribute is handled differently: the RLS MUST NOT apply filters to any notifications it sends, and MUST forward the filter with all fanned-out subscriptions to the notifiers. The RLS MUST also check that there are no filters addressed to the same resource or domain, and if there are it MUST reject the SUBSCRIBE request with a 488 error response.
sections.plainLanguage: A resource list server subscribes on behalf of its client to each member of the list. When a filter is present, it decides what to do with it: it applies list-wide filters itself, passes a filter for one member down to that member, and passes filters for other domains to everyone. Filters for two members of the same list are refused with a 488 response.

sections.title: Generating the NOTIFY
sections.content:
Upon receiving the SUBSCRIBE with the filter, the notifier SHOULD retain the filter as long as the subscription persists. The filter MAY be incorporated within an existing subscription by sending a re-SUBSCRIBE that includes the filter in the body.

The NOTIFY message MAY contain a body that describes the state of the resource, in one of the formats listed in the Accept header field of the SUBSCRIBE, or in the package-specific default if the Accept header field is omitted. Based on the contents of a filter, the processing is as follows. A filter with only a <what> element results in sending the requested resource state information in that element whenever there is a change in the resource state. A filter with only a <trigger> element results in sending all resource state information whenever there is a change in the resource state that matches the triggers. A filter with both elements results in sending the requested resource state information whenever there is a change in the resource state that matches the triggers.

When a filter is disabled by setting the enabled attribute to false, it means the same thing as the absence of that filter, so all state and state changes are reported by issuing a notification to the subscriber. When a filter is re-enabled, the notifier behaves as if the filter had just been placed by the SUBSCRIBE request enabling it.

The input to the content filter is a package-specific XML document. The content is filtered according to the expressions in the <what> element, which indicate the delivered XML elements and attributes. Prefixes of the namespaces of the items to be filtered must be expanded before the filter is applied. In addition to the selected contents, the namespaces of all the selected items are included in the NOTIFY. The items indicated by the expression must be items that the subscriber is authorised to see; if they are not, notifier policy decides, and the RFC recommends that notifiers just ignore the parts of the filter that request unauthorised information.

The resultant XML document MUST be well formed and valid according to the XML schema, which means that all mandatory elements and attributes, along with their values, MUST be included regardless of the expression. If applying the filter results in a document that is not valid, the notifier MUST add elements and attributes from the original document into the newly formulated one in order for it to be valid. If applying the filter results in no content to be delivered, the NOTIFY MUST be sent with empty contents.
sections.plainLanguage: The notifier applies the filter when it builds each notification. The what part selects which parts of the resource state to include, and the trigger part decides which changes are worth sending. The result must still be a valid XML document, so the notifier adds back any mandatory elements the filter removed. Content the subscriber is not allowed to see is left out.

sections.title: Handling Abnormal Cases
sections.content:
In case of an invalid filter definition, where the XML document of the filter is not aligned with the XML schema of the filter format, the notifier rejects the SUBSCRIBE request with a 488 response. A Warning header field in the response may give a better indication of why the filters were not accepted. If the subscription was accepted with a 202 response but the invalid filter was discovered afterwards, a NOTIFY with a subscription-state of value terminated is sent, and an event-reason-value badfilter, introduced by this document, MAY be included. No IANA registration is required for that value.

In case of an erroneous expression in the filter definition, the notifier either ignores the filter definition or terminates the subscription. If a <what> or <trigger> element is empty, the notifier proceeds as if the element did not exist.

The subscriber reads the response to the SUBSCRIBE in the same way. A 200 response indicates that the subscription has been accepted and the filter is accepted, and that a NOTIFY will be sent immediately. A 202 response indicates only that the subscription has been understood and the content type accepted; the filter has not been accepted yet, and its acceptance MAY arrive in a subsequent NOTIFY. A non-200 class final response indicates that no subscription or dialog has been created and no subsequent NOTIFY will be sent. Specifically, a 415 response indicates that the MIME type application/simple-filter+xml is not understood by the notifier, and a 488 response indicates that the content type is understood but some aspects of it were either not understood or not accepted.
sections.plainLanguage: When something is wrong with the filter, the notifier answers 488 and may add a Warning header explaining why. If the problem is found later, it sends a NOTIFY that ends the subscription with the reason badfilter. The subscriber reads the answer to a SUBSCRIBE in the same way: 200 means the filter was accepted, 202 means it has not been accepted yet, and 415 means the notifier does not understand the filter format at all.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The presence of filters in the body of a SIP message has a significant effect on the ways in which the request is handled at a server, so it is especially important that messages containing this extension be authenticated and authorized. Authentication can be achieved using the Digest Authentication mechanism described in RFC 3261. The authorization decision is based on the permissions that the resource, that is the notifier, has given to the watcher.

Processing of requests and looking up filters requires set operations and searches, which can require some amount of computation. This enables a denial-of-service attack in which a user sends requests with substantial numbers of messages with large contents, in the hopes of overloading the server. To counter this, the server can establish a limit on the number of occurrences of the <what>, <changed>, <added> and <removed> elements allowed in the filters. A default limit of 40 is RECOMMENDED, but servers may raise or lower the limit depending on their specific engineered capacity.

Requests can reveal sensitive information about a User Agent's capabilities. If this information is sensitive it SHOULD be encrypted using the SIP S/MIME capabilities of RFC 3851, and all package-specific security measures MUST be followed. Propagating filters in SUBSCRIBE requests to foreign domains reveals sensitive information about a user's resource lists, so it is required that an RLS does not forward a filter that is addressed to a resource that is under the administrative domain of the RLS but that is not on the resource list.

The RFC ends with a warning about what filtering does to the subscriber's view. A filtered document located at a subscriber may project a false reality: if a subscriber asked to be notified when a resource changed his presence state from closed to open but not from open to closed, the subscriber may afterwards be under the false impression that the presence state is open, even long after the resource has changed it to closed. Subscribers therefore need to be sure what they put in a filter, understand what they asked for, and be prepared to be out of sync with the real state of a resource.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages carrying filters should be authenticated and authorized, because filters change how a server handles a request. Filters also cost the server work, so the RFC recommends limiting how many filter elements a request may contain, with 40 as the default. And a filtered view can mislead: a subscriber that asked only for changes to open may still believe the resource is open after it has closed.
